card.title: Stress-Mixture ERC with Sign-Preserving Stress Prior and Drawdown Taper
card.pitch: Blend a sign-preserving one-factor stress covariance into equal-risk-contribution sizing by market absorption, so crises shift risk toward hedges that currently work, under a drawdown taper.
card.mechanism: Σ=(1−p)S+pS*, p the absorption ratio's position between its historical median and 95th percentile. S* keeps the sample's first-component loadings with their signs, amplified toward 0.8 correlation: in flight-to-quality crashes Treasuries load negatively and ERC adds them; in joint stock-bond selloffs (2022) it shifts to gold and commodities. A linear drawdown taper (CPPI, multiplier 1/0.18) caps exposure.
card.rationale: Chow et al. (1999) blend turbulent covariances; Kritzman et al. (2011) link high absorption to drawdowns; Connolly et al. (2005) and Campbell et al. (2017) show stock-bond correlation's sign depends on regime, which the prior follows. Worst case: full calm book loses 9.4% then four 5% weeks; unwinding 18%/week, max DD≈17.8%. Slow 2022-type 15% book loss: DD≈11%. Net ≈3.5–4.5% nominal.
assumptions: Full-exposure ERC book's worst week ≈10% (Oct 2008 estimate −9.4%).
120-day first component carries the current crisis's correlation signs.
failure_modes: Cash lock: at 10% drawdown exposure ≤0.44; recovery ~2–3 years.
A >15% week at full calm exposure breaches 20%.
First component lags a stock-bond correlation flip.
Pre-2010 percentiles thin without proxy splice.
card.cheapest_test: Daily 2006–2025 backtest, index proxies spliced pre-inception, 5bp costs, versus sample-only ERC and uniform-0.8 prior, all with the taper, plus untapered. Kill if max DD ≥20% or the mixture does not beat sample-only ERC on CAGR/maxDD.
card.effort: Medium: ERC solver, shrinkage, eigendecomposition, scheduler; ~200 lines.
sources: Chow, Jacquier, Kritzman, Lowry (1999), Optimal portfolios in good times and bad, Financial Analysts Journal 55(3)
Kritzman, Li, Page, Rigobon (2011), Principal components as a measure of systemic risk, Journal of Portfolio Management 37(4)
Connolly, Stivers, Sun (2005), Stock market uncertainty and the stock-bond return relation, Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 40(1)
Campbell, Sunderam, Viceira (2017), Inflation bets or deflation hedges? The changing risks of nominal bonds, Critical Finance Review 6(2)
Longin, Solnik (2001), Extreme correlation of international equity markets, Journal of Finance 56(2)
Ledoit, Wolf (2004), Honey, I shrunk the sample covariance matrix, Journal of Portfolio Management 30(4)
Spinu (2013), An algorithm for computing risk parity weights, SSRN 2297383
Black, Perold (1992), Theory of constant proportion portfolio insurance, Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control 16(3-4)
card.spec: Tickers SPY IWM EFA EEM IEF TIP LQD GLD DBC VNQ; simple close-to-close returns; σ = sample std ×√252; signals use closes to t−1, fills at close t. S: 120d covariance, Ledoit-Wolf (2004) constant-correlation shrinkage; R its correlation. A=(λ1+λ2)/10 of R; p=clip((A−q50)/(q95−q50),0,1), expanding percentiles of past A, p=0.5 before 504 days. l=√λ1·v1; l*=clip(max(1,√0.8/max|l|)·l,±0.95); S*=D(l*l*′+diag(1−l*²))D, D=diag(max(σ20,σ120)). w=ERC(Σ), equal budgets, Spinu form, cyclic coordinate descent, tol 1e−8. e=min(1, 0.06/√(w′Σw), max(0,1−DD/0.18)), DD from all-time NAV peak. Sessions Mon/Wed/Fri; a closed session moves to the next open non-session day that week, else the previous; weeks ≤3 days trade daily. Per session, turnover (cash counted) ≤6%: first cut exposure by min(6%, current−e), scaling ETF weights proportionally, then move toward target e·w by the uniform fraction the remainder allows. Every session trades (drift makes rebalances nonzero). Weekly ≤18%; 2% drift reserve.

responses.response: Agreed: the 8.5% figure bounded a single 20-day loss, not the drawdown, and the card had no NAV feedback. Added an explicit linear drawdown taper e <= max(0, 1 - DD/B), B = 0.18, with DD measured from the all-time NAV peak. This is CPPI (Black-Perold 1992) with floor = peak x (1 - B) and multiplier m = 1/B = 5.56. The single constant B leaves 2% below the 20% gate; m = 1/B is the unique multiplier that gives exposure 1 at the peak, so no extra parameter is needed. The taper binds by construction whatever sigma_c is. Worst case under the turnover cap: exposure cuts get the whole 6% session budget, so the book can unwind 18% per week. Stylised path starting at peak with exposure 1 and no prior help from the vol target or p. Week 1: book -9.4% (my estimate of the full-exposure calm ERC book in the week of 6-10 Oct 2008). Then four weeks of -5% each (-27% cumulative, about 1.7x my estimate of the ERC book's Sep-Nov 2008 loss of about -16%). Week by week, with exposure averaged linearly within each week: W1 E 0.99 to 0.81, loss 8.5%, DD 8.5%. W2 E 0.81 to 0.63, DD 12.1%. W3 DD 14.8%. W4 E tracks the taper cap, DD 16.6%. W5 DD 17.5%. W6 DD 17.8%. Max is about 17.8%, below 20%. For a slow bear, continuous CPPI gives cushion C = B exp(-L/B). A 15% book loss (my estimate of the 2022 ERC book at full exposure, before the prior's tilt to gold and DBC) gives C = 0.078, so DD is about 10%. Volatility drag on the cushion (m^2 sigma^2/2, about 0.1/yr at 8% book vol) raises this to about 11%. The March 2020 path, with the 6% vol target cutting after week 1, gives about 9% by the same arithmetic. These are hand calculations on approximate ETF returns, not a backtest. The residual breach condition is stated as a failure mode: a single week above about 15% at full calm exposure.

Accepted: uniform rho = 0.8 across all 45 pairs was unsupported for Treasury, TIPS and gold pairs, and it penalised hedges in equity-led crashes. The stress prior is now sign-preserving and one-factor. Loadings are l = sqrt(lambda1) v1 from the current 120-day shrunk correlation. They are scaled by c = max(1, sqrt(0.8)/max|l|), so only the most-exposed pair is pushed to 0.8, which is the equity-equity case where Longin-Solnik applies. C* = l* l*' + diag(1 - l*^2) is positive definite, and the eigenvector's sign is irrelevant because only l l' enters. In a 2008-type crash IEF loads negatively on the first component (its equity correlation was negative then), so the prior makes it a stronger hedge and ERC adds weight to it rather than cutting it. This matches Connolly, Stivers, Sun (2005): stock-bond correlation falls under high equity uncertainty. In 2022 the bonds load positively and are penalised, which matches Campbell, Sunderam, Viceira (2017) on the inflation-regime sign flip. The Longin-Solnik citation is now limited to the equity cluster.

The arithmetic is correct. The card's '55-70% of calm' claim assumed the 6% target binds in calm, and with an unlevered ERC vol of 4-6% it often does not, so the stress-induced cut can be only 10-20%. That claim is withdrawn. Drawdown control no longer rests on the vol target: the linear taper e <= 1 - DD/0.18 binds by construction whatever the calm vol (see the critic-002-09 response for the worst-case path). The mixture's main role is now the re-mix, meaning which assets carry risk in stress, with exposure reduction as a secondary effect. The 6% cap is kept as a speed-of-response device: once 20-day vol spikes it starts the unwind before drawdown accumulates, which is what brings the March 2020 estimate down to about 9%.

The proof is right for the old prior: under equal pairwise correlation, ERC reduces to inverse volatility and discards the cross-asset structure. The new prior is a one-factor model built from the sample's own first component. Under it RC_i = w_i sigma_i [(1 - l_i^2) sigma_i w_i + l_i sum_j l_j sigma_j w_j]. Assets with low or negative loadings therefore contribute less risk per unit weight and receive more weight, so the regime structure is kept rather than erased. In 2022 the first component loads positively on equities, REITs, credit and Treasuries and weakly on GLD and DBC, so rising p tilts risk toward gold and commodities, the diversifiers that worked. In 2008 or early 2020 IEF loads negatively and gains weight. The two crisis types are now treated differently. The residual weakness is lag: the 120-day component needs weeks to register a correlation flip. This is conceded as a failure mode.

The absorption signal now uses the same 120-day shrunk correlation as the covariance (N/T = 0.083, Marchenko-Pastur edge (1 + sqrt(1/12))^2 = 1.66 versus 1.98). It follows Kritzman et al. (2011) in using the top N/5 = 2 eigenvalues: A = (lambda1 + lambda2)/10. This removes the doubly noisy 60-day signal and the associated turnover without information.

The per-session cap is cut to 6.0%, counted with cash as an eleventh weight. This is conservative: under the ETF-only definition, a sale to cash counts only half. Traded weekly turnover is therefore at most 18%, leaving a 2% reserve for price drift under a drift-inclusive reading, which covers the critic's typical estimate of about 1.25%. In extreme weeks drift could exceed 2% if the gate counts drift; I read the gate as measuring traded weight changes.
The spec now lists the tickers explicitly (SPY IWM EFA EEM IEF TIP LQD GLD DBC VNQ), the return definition, the vol annualisation, and the fill convention (signals to close t-1, fill at close t).

The holiday rule is now deterministic: a closed session moves to the next open non-session day in the same week, otherwise to the previous one. Monday holiday moves to Tuesday. Wednesday holiday (Juneteenth, July 4, Christmas) moves to Thursday. Good Friday moves to Thursday. Thanksgiving Thursday needs no move. Collisions are impossible because the target must be a non-session day. Weeks with 3 or fewer trading days trade every day, with at most 3 x 6% = 18% turnover.
